newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan questions U.S. data on output, prices.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan questions U.S. data on output, prices.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan questioned on Wednesday the accuracy of U.S. data on output, prices and productivity, saying current data does not adequately reflect technology changes.

"Insofar as recent productivity growth is concerned, I have a serious question about the quality of the data that we employ to measure output in today's economy," Greenspan said in a speech delivered at a dinner marking The Conference Board's 80th anniversary.
Greenspan said inflation will also be harder to measure in the future.

"How will we measure inflation, and the associated financial market implications, in the 21st century when our data -- using current techniques -- could become increasingly less adequate to trace price trends over time?" he asked.

Greenspan said the economic impact of computerization and other new technologies are difficult to measure. For instance, he said computers are already elevating living standards by "increasing customization to meet particular consumer needs."
"With all the extraordinary technological advances of the past couple of decades, why have our recent productivity data failed to register any improvement?" Greenspan asked.

"To measure productivity and standards of living, we need measures of output. But to measure output, we need to be able to define products clearly and in terms of units that do not change from one period to the next," the Fed chairman said.
The Fed chairman stressed the importance of guaranteeing the future purchasing value of the dollar despite difficulties in price measurements.
Greenspan began his career as an economist in 1948 at the Board, then known as the National Industrial Conference Board.
